prompt: In which language is the simulation written that the Gatling 3.15.1 bundle is set up to run?
hint: Look at the directory the simulations go in.

choices.text: Scala, the language Gatling itself was written in
choices.why: Scala was the original DSL, and it is still offered; the bundle is set up for another.

choices.text: Python, through a plugin bundled with Maven
choices.why: Python is Locust's language, not Gatling's.

choices.text: Java
choices.why: Right. The bundle's simulations live in `src/test/java/`.

choices.text: XML, edited in a window as with JMeter
choices.why: Gatling's tests are code; the XML plan is JMeter's way.

prompt: Why does the `BasicSimulation.java` that ships with the bundle fail in the course's VM?
hint: Where does it send its requests?

choices.text: It is a Scala file, which this bundle's Maven project does not compile
choices.why: It is a Java file, in `src/test/java/example/`.

choices.text: Its requests go to a host on the internet, and the VM test has none
choices.why: Right. A simulation has to ask a system the machine can reach, here the box office.

choices.text: Gatling refuses to run an example class
choices.why: It would run; it would just not reach its host.

choices.text: It has no assertions
choices.why: A simulation with no assertions still runs and reports.

prompt: With `injectOpen(constantUsersPerSec(3).during(15))`, what does each Gatling user do?
hint: Count the arrivals, not the users inside.

choices.text: Loops over the scenario for all 15 seconds, like a k6 virtual user in `constant-vus`
choices.why: That is a closed user. An open injection adds new users instead.

choices.text: Waits until three users have finished, then starts
choices.why: Nothing waits on anybody: arrivals follow the clock.

choices.text: Arrives, does the journey once and leaves
choices.why: Right. Three new ones arrive every second, whatever the box office does.

choices.text: Sends three requests a second until the end
choices.why: The rate is of users arriving; each user sends the requests its journey has.

prompt: In the simulation, `#{show}` is replaced by the value that the ___, called with `.feed(orders)`, handed this user.
A Gatling assertion is crossed. What does the command line see?
hint: The run is a Maven goal.

choices.text: `BUILD FAILURE` from Maven, and exit code 1
choices.why: Right. A failed load test fails the build like a failed unit test.

choices.text: Exit code 99, the same as k6
choices.why: 99 is k6's code. Gatling's runs through Maven, which uses 1.

choices.text: Exit code 0, with `false` printed beside the assertion
choices.why: The line does say `false`, and the exit code is not 0.

choices.text: No exit code, because Gatling only writes the HTML report
choices.why: The report is written either way; the exit code still says pass or fail.

prompt: The simulation injects `rampUsersPerSec(1).to(3).during(5)` and then `constantUsersPerSec(3).during(15)`, and each user sends two requests. The run reported 110 requests. How many users did Gatling start?
About a third of the seats booked at random were already taken, yet the `KO` column stayed at 0. Why?
hint: What does the booking's check accept?

choices.text: Gatling counts a 4xx answer as OK unless told otherwise
choices.why: A status the check does not accept is KO, 4xx or not.

choices.text: The check on the booking accepts 409 as well as 201
choices.why: Right. A 409 is the box office refusing correctly, and the check says so.

choices.text: The box office answered 201 even for taken seats
choices.why: It answers 409 for a seat already sold, as lesson 1 showed.

choices.text: KO counts only connections that were refused
choices.why: KO counts any request that failed a check.

prompt: Match each piece of the simulation to what it does.

pairs.right: hands the user a show and a seat picked at random
the think time between looking and booking
starts new users at a rate, whatever the server does
decides whether the Maven build passes

right_distractors: keeps a fixed number of users inside the system

prompt: A Locust user has `@task(3)` on one method and `@task(1)` on another. What share of its tasks is the second one?

choices.text: One in three
choices.why: That would be weights of 2 and 1.

choices.text: One in four
choices.why: Right. 1 out of a total weight of 4.

choices.text: One in two, until the first has run three times
choices.why: The weights are a chance per pick, not a schedule.

choices.text: A third of the run's duration
choices.why: Weights share the picks, not the time.

prompt: Why does `book_a_seat` call `r.success()` when the box office answers 409?
hint: What does Locust do by default with a status of 400 or more?

choices.text: Locust would retry the booking until it got a 201
choices.why: Locust retries nothing; the call only decides how the answer is counted.

choices.text: Without it, every taken seat would be counted as a failure, though the box office answered correctly
choices.why: Right. Locust counts a status of 400 or more as failed unless told otherwise.

choices.text: `success()` makes the request faster
choices.why: It changes the statistics, not the request.

choices.text: A 409 has no body, and Locust needs one
choices.why: The 409 does have a body, and Locust needs none.

prompt: A locustfile has no `quitting` hook. Its run finishes with no failed request and a 95th percentile of 900 ms. What exit code does Locust give?
hint: What does Locust judge on its own?

choices.text: 1, because the run was slow
choices.why: Locust has no idea what slow means here; nobody wrote it down.

choices.text: 99, as k6 does for a crossed threshold
choices.why: 99 is k6's code, and Locust has no thresholds.
Right. Without a hook, Locust's exit code depends only on whether a request failed.

choices.text: 2, a warning
choices.why: Locust uses no such code for slowness.

prompt: Put the life of one Locust user in order, from the moment it is started.
items: a task is picked by its weight
the task's request is sent and counted
wait_time passes before the next pick

prompt: What do `-u 10 -r 2` mean on the Locust command line?

choices.text: 10 requests a second, 2 of them bookings
choices.why: `-u` counts users, not requests.

choices.text: 10 users in all, started 2 a second
choices.why: Right. All ten were running after about five seconds.

choices.text: 10 seconds of test, after 2 seconds of warm-up
choices.why: `-t 20s` is the duration.

choices.text: 10 tasks per user, 2 at a time
choices.why: A user runs tasks one at a time, for as long as the test lasts.

prompt: Which of these write an open model, one where new work arrives at a rate whatever the server does? Choose every one that applies.
hint: Who decides when the next piece of work starts?

choices.text: Gatling's `injectOpen(constantUsersPerSec(5))`
choices.why: Right. Five users arrive every second.

choices.text: k6's `constant-arrival-rate` executor
choices.why: Right. Iterations start on the clock.

choices.text: Locust users with `wait_time = between(1, 3)`
choices.why: Each user waits for its answer and then for its wait: a closed loop.

choices.text: k6's `vus: 5, duration: '10s'`
choices.why: That is `constant-vus`: five loops, each waiting on the server.

prompt: A report says "20 users" for a Gatling run and "20 users" for a Locust run against the same system. What can you conclude about the two loads?
hint: What is a user in each tool?

choices.text: They are the same load, written in two languages
choices.why: The word is the same; the meaning is not.

choices.text: Locust's is heavier, because Python is slower
choices.why: The language of the generator does not decide the load.

choices.text: Nothing yet: one is arrivals a second, the other is users inside at once
choices.why: Right. Convert both to requests a second before comparing.

choices.text: Gatling's is heavier, because Java is faster than Python at sending requests
choices.why: Speed of the generator is not what the number counts.

prompt: A Python team must test "30 requests a second" with Locust, against a page that answers in about 100 ms. Which user setup holds that rate as written?
hint: A wait that paces each user rather than following each answer.

choices.text: 30 users with `wait_time = between(1, 3)`
choices.why: That is about one request every two seconds each, 15 a second, and less as answers slow.

choices.text: 3 users with no `wait_time` at all
choices.why: Each loops as fast as the answers allow: the rate is whatever the server gives.

choices.text: 30 users with `wait_time = constant_throughput(1)`
choices.why: Right. Each user is paced to one task a second, so 30 users hold 30 a second while answers stay under a second.

choices.text: 1 user started with `-r 30`
choices.why: `-r` is how fast users start, not how often they ask.

prompt: The box office stalls for five seconds in the middle of two runs: one Gatling run with `injectOpen`, one Locust run with 10 users. What does the stall do to the number of users inside each run?

choices.text: Ten in Locust, and climbing in Gatling as arrivals keep coming
choices.why: Right. Locust's ten wait; Gatling keeps starting new users who also wait.

choices.text: It falls in both Gatling and Locust, as the generator slows with the server
choices.why: Locust's count is fixed at 10; Gatling's arrivals do not slow down.

choices.text: It rises in both Gatling and Locust
choices.why: Locust never has more than the 10 users it was told to run.

choices.text: Gatling and Locust both keep the same count
choices.why: Gatling's arrivals pile up inside while nobody leaves.

prompt: A colleague ports lesson 5's k6 script to Gatling and keeps `p(95)<200` only as a global assertion. The bookings' 95th percentile is 250 ms and the shows' 40 ms, and the build passes. What is the better assertion?
hint: Which operation does lesson 1's requirement name?

choices.text: Remove the assertions, and read the HTML report by hand after every run instead
choices.why: Then nothing fails the build, and somebody has to remember to look.

choices.text: One on `details("show")` at 200 ms, and a separate one for the POST
choices.why: Right. Lesson 1's requirement is about one operation; a global percentile mixes the two.

choices.text: A global `mean` under 200 ms
choices.why: A mean hides the slow tail that the percentile is there to catch.

choices.text: Raise the limit to 300 so that both pass
choices.why: Moving the threshold to fit the result is writing the requirement after the test.
